nodes.label: The end of the Ptolemies
nodes.full: Actium (31) and Octavian's invasion (30) ended the Ptolemaic dynasty; the annexation that opens this folio is the direct consequence.
nodes.src: background — see the folio egypt-332bc-30bc (Ptolemaic Egypt)

nodes.label: Rome and the Emperor
nodes.full: The city of Rome that Egypt's grain fed, and the emperor whose closed personal possession the province was — the external centre around which the whole folio turns.
nodes.src: background — added on review; Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980)

nodes.label: The kingdom of Meroe
nodes.full: The independent Nubian kingdom on the upper Nile, with which Rome fought a war in 25–22 BC and then kept a peaceful frontier for nearly three centuries before Meroe's decline.
nodes.src: background — added on review; Török, Between Two Worlds (2009)

nodes.label: Christian and Byzantine Egypt
nodes.full: Diocletian's reorganisation and the Great Persecution open the next era — a Christianising Egypt of monks, bishops and the see of Alexandria, ruled from Constantinople.
nodes.src: background — added on review; belongs to the next folio; Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993)

nodes.label: Augustus annexes Egypt
nodes.full: Octavian took Egypt as spoils and kept it apart: it became neither a normal province nor his personal estate exactly, but a domain governed for the emperor by a hand-picked equestrian prefect, with three legions, and closed to Roman senators and leading equestrians who could not enter without the emperor's permission. Alexandria was left without a town council. The reason was the grain and the treasury — no rival could be allowed a base there.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 2.59, Histories 1.11; Cassius Dio 51.17; Strabo 17.1.12–13. Alan K. Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986) pp.37–52; Livia Capponi, Augustan Egypt (2005).

nodes.label: Cornelius Gallus — the first prefect, and a warning
nodes.full: The poet-soldier Gaius Cornelius Gallus, Augustus' first prefect, put down a tax revolt in the Thebaid and boasted of it on a trilingual victory stela at Philae — 'no king or Roman had penetrated so far'. The self-promotion, and reports of it, cost him Augustus' friendship; recalled and prosecuted, he killed himself in 26 BC. His fall set the tone: the prefecture was powerful, watched, and lethal to anyone who forgot he served the emperor.
nodes.src: Gallus stela (Philae; now Cairo): F. Hoffmann, M. Minas-Nerpel & S. Pfeiffer, Die dreisprachige Stele des C. Cornelius Gallus (2009). Suetonius, Augustus 66; Dio 53.23–24; Ovid, Amores 3.9.

nodes.label: Germanicus and the rule that the family stays out
nodes.full: Tiberius' heir Germanicus toured Egypt in 19 AD without imperial leave — sailing up the Nile, reading the Colossi of Memnon, and opening the state granaries to lower the price of bread in Alexandria. Tiberius rebuked him sharply, less for the sightseeing than for entering the province at all and for playing the popular benefactor with Rome's grain. The episode fixed the principle that no member of the imperial house set foot in Egypt uninvited.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 2.59–61; the edict of Germanicus (P. Oxy. XXV 2435) declining divine honours. Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986) pp.40–41.

nodes.label: Gaius and the Alexandrian crisis
nodes.full: Under Gaius (Caligula) the long friction between Alexandria's Greeks and its large Jewish community broke into open violence in 38, with the connivance of the prefect Flaccus. Both sides sent embassies to Rome — the Jewish one led by the philosopher Philo, the Greek one by the scholar Apion — and Philo's account of the audience with a distracted, hostile emperor is one of antiquity's sharpest portraits of imperial court politics.
nodes.src: Philo, In Flaccum and Legatio ad Gaium. Josephus, Antiquities 18.257–60. The 'Letter of Claudius to the Alexandrians' (P. Lond. 1912), 41 AD, on the aftermath.

nodes.label: Vespasian proclaimed at Alexandria
nodes.full: On 1 July 69, in the year of four emperors, the prefect Tiberius Julius Alexander had the Egyptian legions swear allegiance to Vespasian — the first formal declaration of his bid for the throne, and the date he later counted as his accession. Vespasian wintered in Alexandria holding the grain supply as leverage over Rome, and the sources have him work healing miracles there, curing a blind man with spittle and a lame man with his heel, in the manner expected of a divinely favoured ruler.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Histories 3.48, 4.81–82; Suetonius, Vespasian 7; Dio 65.8. The oath: P. Oxy. — the accession-dating shift. Kevin Butcher, Roman Syria and the Near East (2003) for context.

nodes.label: Trajan — the canal, the fort and the Jewish war
nodes.full: Trajan re-dredged the silted Nile–Red Sea canal, so that it was known for centuries as 'Trajan's River', to feed the Red Sea trade and the eastern campaigns. He rebuilt the legionary fortress at Babylon, at the apex of the Delta — the walls that still stand in Old Cairo. And his reign ended amid the Diaspora Revolt of 115–117, the messianic Jewish rising that consumed the Jewish communities of Egypt.
nodes.src: Trajan's canal: P. Oxy. and the Antinoopolis milestones; John Ball, Egypt in the Classical Geographers (1942). Babylon fortress: Peter Sheehan, Babylon of Egypt (2010). The revolt: see Conflict.

nodes.label: Hadrian's Nile journey and Antinoopolis
nodes.full: Hadrian toured Egypt in 130–131 with his court and his favourite, the Bithynian youth Antinous, who drowned in the Nile near Hermopolis in October 130 in unclear circumstances. Hadrian founded a Greek city, Antinoopolis, on the east bank at the spot, established games and a cult of the deified Antinous that spread across the empire, and rode out to hear the Colossi of Memnon sing at dawn — where his companion Julia Balbilla left verse graffiti still on the statue's leg.
nodes.src: Historia Augusta, Hadrian 14; the Obelisk of Antinous (Rome). Antinoopolis: Rosario Pintaudi (ed.), Antinoupolis (2008– ). Memnon inscriptions: André Bernand & Étienne Bernand, Les inscriptions grecques et latines du Colosse de Memnon (1960).

nodes.label: Marcus Aurelius, the Boukoloi and Avidius Cassius
nodes.full: In 172 the 'herdsmen' of the Delta swamps, the Boukoloi, rose under a priest, wiped out a Roman detachment by a ruse, and beat the Alexandrian militia in open battle before the Syrian governor Avidius Cassius crushed them by setting the rebel factions against each other. Three years later Cassius, on a false report that Marcus Aurelius had died, had himself proclaimed emperor with Egyptian support; the real Marcus was very much alive, and Cassius was killed by his own officers within months.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 72.4 (Boukoloi), 72.22–27 (Avidius Cassius); Historia Augusta, Avidius Cassius. The Boukoloi also appear in the novel of Achilles Tatius 3–4.

nodes.label: Septimius Severus gives the cities councils
nodes.full: Septimius Severus toured Egypt for over a year, visiting the tomb of Alexander and the antiquities of the Nile and, at Abydos, closing the oracle-temple that drew crowds seeking political prophecy. His lasting act was administrative: he gave Alexandria, and then the capital of each nome, a town council (boule) of local property-owners for the first time in Roman rule, shifting the burden and some of the power of local government onto a curial class.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 76.13; Historia Augusta, Severus 17. The grant of councils: the Severan reorganisation, A.K. Bowman, The Town Councils of Roman Egypt (1971).

nodes.label: Caracalla's citizenship and Caracalla's massacre
nodes.full: Caracalla's Antonine Constitution of 212 made almost every free inhabitant of the empire a Roman citizen — a change that in Egypt cut across the carefully graded local status system and slowly eroded the distinction between 'Hellene' and 'Egyptian'. In 215, visiting Alexandria and stung by the citizens' jokes about him, he had his soldiers cordon and cut down a large number of the city's young men, then quartered troops in the houses and banned the assemblies.
nodes.src: Antonine Constitution: P. Giss. 40; Dio 78.9. The massacre: Dio 78.22–23; Herodian 4.9. Fergus Millar, The Roman Near East (1993).

nodes.label: The third-century crisis in Egypt
nodes.full: Egypt shared the empire's mid-century collapse. A pandemic — the 'Plague of Cyprian' — struck from about 249; the silver content of the Alexandrian coinage crashed and prices multiplied; the burden of unpaid public services (liturgies) drove men to flee their villages (anachoresis); and papyri from the Faiyum show tax districts asking to be relieved of ruined, deserted land. Some of the drained-marsh villages settled under the Ptolemies were abandoned for good.
nodes.src: Kyle Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017) on the Plague of Cyprian in the papyri. Village decline: Roger Bagnall, 'Agricultural Productivity and Taxation in Later Roman Egypt', TAPA 115 (1985); the Karanis and Soknopaiou Nesos evidence.

nodes.label: The Palmyrene occupation of Egypt
nodes.full: Around 270, forces of the Palmyrene queen Zenobia under the general Zabdas, helped by a local partisan, seized Egypt and held it in the name of her son Vaballathus, whose name appears alongside Aurelian's on the Alexandrian coinage until the break. Aurelian recovered the province in 272 in the campaign that also destroyed Palmyra. The fighting damaged the palace quarter of Alexandria, and a merchant named Firmus with desert connections mounted a brief revolt in the aftermath.
nodes.src: Historia Augusta, Aurelian 32, Firmus 3; Zosimus 1.44. The Vaballathus/Aurelian coinage of Alexandria. Richard Stoneman, Palmyra and its Empire (1992); Andrew Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999).

nodes.label: Diocletian — the siege and the reorganisation
nodes.full: When Lucius Domitius Domitianus revolted in 297 with a subordinate, Achilleus, Diocletian besieged Alexandria for eight months and stormed it in 298. He then reordered the province root and branch: Egypt was split into smaller provinces under a new hierarchy, the annual tax cycle (indiction) and a reformed assessment were imposed, the separate Alexandrian coinage was abolished for the imperial denominations, and the southern frontier was pulled back from the Dodekaschoinos to the First Cataract by treaty with the desert peoples.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 1.19 (the frontier withdrawal); the Panopolis papyri (P. Beatty Panop.) on the reorganised administration. J.D. Thomas, 'The Introduction of Dediticii...', and the 'Great Persecution' (see Belief).

nodes.label: The prefecture of Egypt
nodes.full: The praefectus Aegypti was the most powerful equestrian post in the empire: commander of the legions, supreme judge, head of finance, and the emperor's stand-in. He issued an edict on taking office, toured the country each year holding assizes (the conventus) that drew thousands of petitioners, and controlled — through the 'special account', the idios logos — confiscated property and the rules of personal status. Holders ranged from the Jewish apostate Tiberius Julius Alexander to men who later governed Rome itself.
nodes.src: Prefect's edict: e.g. the edict of Tiberius Julius Alexander (OGIS 669), 68 AD. Gnomon of the Idios Logos (BGU V 1210). Guido Bastianini, 'Lista dei prefetti d'Egitto', ZPE 17 (1975) and updates.

nodes.label: The war with Meroe
nodes.full: Soon after annexation, the armies of the Kandake (queen) of Meroe, Amanirenas, raided over the new frontier, sacked Aswan, Elephantine and Philae, and carried off statues of Augustus — one bronze head was buried under the threshold of a Meroë temple so worshippers would tread on the emperor forever. The prefect Petronius struck back, took Napata and razed it, then negotiated a frontier treaty that held the peace at the First Cataract for three centuries.
nodes.src: Strabo 17.1.53–54; Res Gestae 26; Pliny 6.181–82. The 'Meroë Head' of Augustus (British Museum, from Garstang's 1910 excavation). László Török, Between Two Worlds (2009) pp.427–55.

nodes.label: The Thebaid tax revolt
nodes.full: Within a year of the Roman takeover, Upper Egypt rose against the new tax demands. Cornelius Gallus put the revolt down in fifteen days by his own account, taking Coptos and other towns, and set it at the head of the boasts on his Philae stela. It was the first of a long series in which Roman fiscal pressure — heavier and more relentlessly collected than the Ptolemies' — met organised Egyptian resistance.
nodes.src: Gallus stela (Philae); Strabo 17.1.53; Dio 53.23. Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986) pp.37–40.

nodes.label: The Alexandrian pogrom of 38 AD
nodes.full: In the summer of 38 the Greek population of Alexandria, with the prefect Flaccus standing aside, attacked the Jewish community: Jews were driven into a single crowded quarter, their shops looted, their meeting-houses seized and images of the emperor set up in them, and the council of elders publicly flogged. Philo, who lived through it and led the community's embassy to Rome, wrote two treatises on the events — the earliest detailed account of an organised assault on a Jewish population.
nodes.src: Philo, In Flaccum, Legatio ad Gaium. Sandra Gambetti, The Alexandrian Riots of 38 C.E. and the Persecution of the Jews (2009).

nodes.label: The Diaspora Revolt
nodes.full: While Trajan campaigned in the east, the Jewish communities of Cyrene, Egypt and Cyprus rose in a coordinated, messianically charged war against their Greek neighbours and the Roman state. In Egypt the fighting raged across the countryside for two years — papyri record burned estates, pitched battles, and villagers conscripted against the rebels — until the general Marcius Turbo suppressed it with heavy force. The once-great Jewish population of Egypt was effectively wiped out and did not recover for centuries.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 68.32; Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica 4.2. The papyrological dossier: Corpus Papyrorum Judaicarum II 435–450; Miriam Pucci Ben Zeev, Diaspora Judaism in Turmoil, 116/117 CE (2005).

nodes.label: The revolt of the Boukoloi
nodes.full: The 'herdsmen' of the papyrus marshes of the western Delta rebelled under a priest called Isidorus, opened by luring a Roman patrol ashore with a fake ransom and killing them, then defeated the troops of Alexandria in the field and nearly took the city. The Syrian governor Avidius Cassius put it down not by battle but by exploiting the rebels' own divisions. The marsh-dwellers had a fearsome literary reputation; the novelist Achilles Tatius sets a kidnapping among them.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 72.4; Historia Augusta, Marcus 21. Achilles Tatius, Leucippe and Clitophon 3.9–4.18. Analysis: Andrew Alföldi and, more recently, Kostas Vlassopoulos on the trope.

nodes.label: Caracalla's massacre at Alexandria
nodes.full: Caracalla, resentful of Alexandrian jokes about him and his mother, entered the city under a show of goodwill, summoned the young men to a parade ground on the pretext of enrolling them in a legion, and had his soldiers surround and kill them in large numbers. He then billeted troops through the city, split it with a wall, closed the shows and the common messes, and expelled non-residents. It was the single worst day Alexandria suffered under Roman rule.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 78.22–23; Herodian 4.8–9. Christopher Haas, Alexandria in Late Antiquity (1997) pp.68–70.

nodes.label: The Palmyrene war and Aurelian's reconquest
nodes.full: Zenobia's Palmyrene forces occupied Egypt around 270, and for two years the province was governed in the name of her son. Aurelian's reconquest in 272 involved fighting in and around Alexandria that wrecked the Brucheion, the palace-and-Museum quarter, from which the ancient scholarly institution never fully recovered. A local usurper, the merchant Firmus, was suppressed soon after.
nodes.src: Zosimus 1.44, 1.61; Historia Augusta, Firmus 3 (partly fictionalised). The Brucheion's fate: Ammianus Marcellinus 22.16.15; Haas, Alexandria in Late Antiquity (1997).

nodes.label: The siege of Alexandria, 297–298
nodes.full: Lucius Domitius Domitianus, backed by the corrector Achilleus, was proclaimed Augustus in Egypt in mid-297, striking his own coinage. Diocletian came in person, besieged Alexandria for eight months, cut its aqueduct, and stormed it in the spring of 298, allowing a sack. The granite column later miscalled 'Pompey's Pillar' was raised by the city to the victorious emperor. The reorganisation of the province followed at once.
nodes.src: P. Oxy. and the Domitianus coinage; the Panopolis papyri. Pompey's Pillar dedication: CIL III 12047. Timothy Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982) pp.11–12, 62.

nodes.label: The closed province
nodes.full: Egypt was governed unlike any other province: an equestrian prefect stood in for the emperor as commander, supreme judge and head of finance, assisted by a chief justice (iuridicus), a finance procurator, and the idios logos overseeing confiscations and status. Senators and top equestrians could not enter without leave. The whole apparatus existed to keep the grain flowing to Rome and to keep any rival from using the province as a base.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Histories 1.11; Strabo 17.1.12. Naphtali Lewis, Life in Egypt under Roman Rule (1983) pp.16–35; Alan K. Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986) pp.66–89.

nodes.label: The census, the records and the poll tax
nodes.full: Rome ran the first regular census in history here: every fourteen years each household filed a return listing its members and property, updated by birth, death and property declarations. On this base sat the poll tax (laographia), levied on almost every man between fourteen and sixty-two, and a battery of taxes on land, trades and transactions. The paperwork — returns, receipts, ledgers, petitions — survives in such quantity that Roman Egypt is the best-documented society before the modern age.
nodes.src: Roger Bagnall & Bruce Frier, The Demography of Roman Egypt (1994). Poll tax: S.L. Wallace, Taxation in Egypt from Augustus to Diocletian (1938). The Karanis tax rolls: H.C. Youtie & O.M. Pearl, Papyri and Ostraca from Karanis (1939–44).

nodes.label: The status hierarchy
nodes.full: Roman Egypt sorted its people into legal grades, each with its own tax rate and rights: Roman citizens at the top, then citizens of the three Greek cities, then the 'metropolites' — privileged residents of a nome capital who paid a reduced poll tax — and below them the mass of 'Egyptians' paying the full rate. Membership was checked at age fourteen in a status scrutiny (epikrisis), and the exclusive 'from-the-gymnasium' class kept sealed membership lists. Ethnicity had become a fiscal category.
nodes.src: Claire Préaux and, definitively, the epikrisis and gymnasial documents: P. Oxy. and the studies of Peter van Minnen on the gymnasial women and elite of the metropoleis of Roman Egypt (2002).

nodes.label: The liturgy system
nodes.full: Local government ran on compulsory unpaid service. Men with enough property were conscripted, by lot from the census lists, to collect taxes, guard the granaries, supervise the dike corvée, or serve as village head — personally liable for any shortfall. As the burden grew heavier in the second and third centuries, the assigned men increasingly abandoned their homes and land to escape it (anachoresis), and the system that held the countryside together began to unravel.
nodes.src: Naphtali Lewis, The Compulsory Public Services of Roman Egypt (1982, 2nd ed. 1997). Anachoresis and its fiscal consequences: Roger Bagnall in Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993) pp.148–60.

nodes.label: Roman law and Egyptian custom
nodes.full: Two legal worlds ran in parallel. The prefect's court and his annual assize circuit applied Roman law to citizens and, flexibly, judged everyone else; the Gnomon of the Idios Logos codified the penalties for crossing status and inheritance lines. Local practice was tolerated where it did not offend Roman order — including the full-sibling marriage that census returns show was genuinely common among ordinary Egyptian families in this period, the only well-documented society where it was.
nodes.src: Gnomon of the Idios Logos (BGU V 1210). Sibling marriage: Keith Hopkins, 'Brother-Sister Marriage in Roman Egypt', Comparative Studies in Society and History 22 (1980); Sabine Huebner, 'Brother-Sister Marriage in Roman Egypt: a Curiosity of Humankind or a Widespread Family Strategy?', JRS 97 (2007).

nodes.label: The nome, the metropolis and the council
nodes.full: Egypt kept its ancient division into about forty nomes, each now under a civilian strategos appointed by the prefect, a royal scribe, and a nome capital (metropolis) with Greek-style institutions. In 200/201 Septimius Severus gave Alexandria and every metropolis a town council of local landowners, transferring the day-to-day running — and the financial liability — of the district onto a curial class, the model of civic government used across the rest of the empire.
nodes.src: A.K. Bowman, The Town Councils of Roman Egypt (1971). The strategos's archive: e.g. P. Oxy. and the dossier of Apollonios strategos of the Apollonopolite Heptakomias (115–120 AD).

nodes.label: The army of Egypt
nodes.full: Two, later one, legions garrisoned Egypt from the base camp of Nikopolis east of Alexandria, with auxiliary cohorts and cavalry along the Nile and, from Diocletian, a legion at Babylon. Detachments manned the desert road forts (praesidia) that guarded the routes to the Red Sea and the quarries, escorted the grain and the tax silver, policed the villages, and supervised the quarry gangs. Roman military ostraca from these forts document the whole system in daily notes about water, wheat and passing traffic.
nodes.src: Michael Speidel, 'The Roman Army in Egypt', ANRW II.10.1 (1988). Desert forts: Hélène Cuvigny (ed.), La route de Myos Hormos (2003) and the Krokodilô and Didymoi ostraca.

nodes.label: The pharaoh who never came
nodes.full: The Egyptian temples carried on carving the reigning Roman emperor as king of Egypt — Augustus, Tiberius, Nero, Domitian, Trajan, Antoninus, on to Decius — in full pharaonic regalia, his name in a cartouche, offering to the gods, though no emperor after the annexation visited a sanctuary of the chora. Rome completed the last new Egyptian temples, at Esna, Kom Ombo and Dendera, while at the same time regulating the priesthood into decline: fixed numbers, licensed circumcision, inventoried property, a state salary in place of endowments, and an imperial official over all the cults.
nodes.src: Emperor cartouches: the temple building texts; Martina Minas-Nerpel & Stefan Pfeiffer on the Roman-period temples. Priestly regulation: the Gnomon of the Idios Logos; David Frankfurter, Religion in Roman Egypt (1998) pp.27–36.

nodes.label: Isis conquers the empire
nodes.full: The Egyptian gods travelled with the sailors, soldiers and traders of the empire. Temples of Isis, Serapis, Harpocrates and Anubis went up in Rome, Italy, Gaul, Britain and along the Danube; the mysteries of Isis offered personal salvation and rebirth; and Apuleius' novel The Golden Ass closes with a shimmering first-person account of an initiation at Kenchreai. To the wider Roman world Egypt was the source of the deepest and strangest wisdom.
nodes.src: Apuleius, Metamorphoses 11. R.E. Witt, Isis in the Ancient World (1971); Laurent Bricault, Atlas de la diffusion des cultes isiaques (2001) and Isis, Dame des flots (2006).

nodes.label: Christianity comes to Alexandria and the villages
nodes.full: Christian tradition credits the evangelist Mark with founding the church of Alexandria in the 60s, but the movement is first visible in the Egyptian countryside: the oldest surviving fragments of the New Testament — scraps of John, Matthew and Luke — come from the rubbish mounds and cartonnage of the chora and date to the second century. From the city the faith spread up the Nile, and the need to reach non-Greek speakers drove the first translations of scripture into the Egyptian language, written in Greek letters: Coptic.
nodes.src: Earliest NT papyri: P52 (John, John Rylands), P66, P75. Birger Pearson, Gnosticism and Christianity in Roman and Coptic Egypt (2004); C.H. Roberts, Manuscript, Society and Belief in Early Christian Egypt (1979).

nodes.label: The Catechetical School
nodes.full: Alexandrian Christianity developed as a scholarly, philosophical tradition. Pantaenus, then Clement — whose works quote Greek poetry and philosophy on every page while arguing for Christ as the true Logos — and then Origen, the most prolific author of the ancient church: the Hexapla setting six versions of the Old Testament in columns, systematic theology in On First Principles, and thousands of homilies and commentaries. It set the intellectual template for Greek Christian thought.
nodes.src: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica 5.10–11, 6. Clement: the Protrepticus, Paedagogus, Stromateis. Origen: On First Principles, Contra Celsum. Ronald Heine, Origen: Scholarship in the Service of the Church (2010).

nodes.label: Gnostics and Hermetists
nodes.full: Second-century Alexandria was the great laboratory of religious synthesis. The Gnostic teachers Basilides and Valentinus built elaborate systems of a flawed creation and a hidden saving knowledge; Coptic translations of such texts were buried near Nag Hammadi and recovered in 1945. In the same milieu, philosophical dialogues in Greek — the Hermetic corpus, headed by the Poimandres — put a doctrine of the soul's ascent to God under the name of the Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus, Thoth.
nodes.src: Nag Hammadi library: James Robinson (ed.), The Nag Hammadi Library in English (1988). Hermetica: Brian Copenhaver's translation (1992); Garth Fowden, The Egyptian Hermes (1986). Gnostic teachers: Bentley Layton, The Gnostic Scriptures (1987).

nodes.label: The persecutions and the Era of the Martyrs
nodes.full: Rome moved against the Egyptian church in waves. Septimius Severus' 202 ban on conversion killed Origen's father Leonides and the catechumen Potamiaena; the Decian order of 250 required everyone to sacrifice and receive a certificate, and dozens of these libelli survive on papyrus from Egyptian villages, the only place they do; and the Great Persecution begun in 303 fell heaviest of all here. Egyptian Christians dated their calendar's start to Diocletian's accession in 284 — the Era of the Martyrs, still used by the Coptic Church.
nodes.src: Decian libelli: J.R. Knipfing, 'The Libelli of the Decian Persecution', Harvard Theological Review 16 (1923); P. Oxy. and P. Mich. examples. Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica 6.1–5, 8. The Great Persecution: Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine and HE 8.

nodes.label: Gods, oracles, horoscopes and spells in daily life
nodes.full: Below the debates of the schools, ordinary religious practice thickened. Households kept terracotta figures of Bes, Harpocrates and Isis-with-grain; people still put yes-or-no questions to temple oracles on paired papyrus slips; the personal horoscope became routine, and hundreds survive; and long handbooks of practical magic — the Greek and Demotic magical papyri, mixing Egyptian, Greek and Jewish names of power — were compiled, alongside amulets against fever and the evil eye and the still-continuing, if declining, mummification of sacred animals.
nodes.src: Magical papyri: Hans Dieter Betz (ed.), The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation (1986); the London-Leiden Demotic Magical Papyrus. Oracle tickets: P. Oxy. Horoscopes: Otto Neugebauer & H.B. van Hoesen, Greek Horoscopes (1959). David Frankfurter, Religion in Roman Egypt (1998).

nodes.label: The Faiyum mummy portraits
nodes.full: For two centuries, well-off families in the Faiyum and elsewhere commissioned a lifelike portrait of the deceased — painted in coloured beeswax or tempera on a thin wooden panel — and had it bound into the mummy wrappings over the face. The style is Greco-Roman naturalism, the setting an Egyptian burial. Over a thousand survive, more than any other body of ancient panel painting, and they look out with an immediacy nothing else from antiquity matches.
nodes.src: Susan Walker & Morris Bierbrier (eds.), Ancient Faces: Mummy Portraits from Roman Egypt (1997); Barbara Borg, Mumienporträts (1996). Petrie's Hawara excavations (1888, 1911).

nodes.label: The last Egyptian temples
nodes.full: Egyptian temple-building finished under the emperors. The pillared entrance hall (pronaos) at Esna was decorated with hymns and priestly lore down to the mid-third century; Kom Ombo, Kalabsha in Nubia, the birth-house and roof chapels of Dendera, and the kiosk on Philae belong to the same last phase. The craftsmen still cut hieroglyphs and carved a Roman emperor as pharaoh, but the tradition was closing: Esna's is among the very last monumental hieroglyphic decoration ever done.
nodes.src: Serge Sauneron, Le temple d'Esna (1959– ) and Quatre campagnes à Esna (1959). Dieter Arnold, Temples of the Last Pharaohs (1999) pp.225–86 covers the Roman-period work.

nodes.label: Roman Alexandria
nodes.full: Alexandria kept its Ptolemaic bones and gained a Roman skin: the Caesareum temple with its pair of obelisks later called 'Cleopatra's Needles', a long aqueduct feeding rock-cut cisterns, a theatre, and the vast painted rock-cut tombs of Kom el-Shoqafa, where a dead man is shown at once as an Egyptian mummy tended by Anubis and as a Roman in a toga. The granite column raised for Diocletian, misnamed 'Pompey's Pillar', still dominates the old acropolis.
nodes.src: Judith McKenzie, The Architecture of Alexandria and Egypt (2007). Kom el-Shoqafa: Marjorie Venit, Monumental Tombs of Ancient Alexandria (2002). The submerged city: Franck Goddio's Portus Magnus survey.

nodes.label: Lost Greek literature from the rubbish mounds
nodes.full: The dry town dumps of the Nile chora preserved what the medieval manuscript tradition lost. From Oxyrhynchus alone have come new plays of Menander, poems of Sappho and Alcaeus, the victory odes of Bacchylides, works of Callimachus, historical fragments and the earliest Christian texts — recovered from thousands of discarded rolls and codices. They also show the reading life of the Greek-speaking metropolite: private libraries, book dealers, school exercises, and requests to borrow a volume from a friend.
nodes.src: The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, 80+ volumes (Egypt Exploration Society, 1898– ). Peter Parsons, City of the Sharp-Nosed Fish (2007); William Johnson, Bookrolls and Scribes in Oxyrhynchus (2004).

nodes.label: The making of Coptic
nodes.full: The Egyptian language was written in a new way: the Greek alphabet plus a handful of extra letters taken from Demotic, spelling out the spoken tongue with vowels for the first time. It began with 'Old Coptic' glosses in magical and astrological texts, where getting the pronunciation exact mattered, and then, as Christianity reached villagers who knew no Greek, became the script of Bible translations and monastic letters. The old scripts faded in step: Demotic and hieroglyphic writing was nearly gone by 300.
nodes.src: Bentley Layton, A Coptic Grammar (2000), intro. Old Coptic: J. Osing, Der spätägyptische Papyrus BM 10808 (1976); the London-Leiden magical papyrus glosses. Roger Bagnall, Everyday Writing in the Graeco-Roman East (2011).

nodes.label: The games, the pantomime and the water-organ
nodes.full: Roman Egypt kept a full public entertainment culture. Alexandria hosted sacred games on the Greek model, and Hadrian founded the Antinoeia contests at Antinoopolis; the touring guild of 'Artists of Dionysus' still moved between cities with imperial privileges; the pantomime dancer with his musicians was the star turn of the age. The Alexandrian invention of the water-organ, the hydraulis, is pictured on the city's lamps and terracottas and spread with the games across the empire.
nodes.src: Sofie Remijsen, The End of Greek Athletics in Late Antiquity (2015) on the games. Technitai: the Antinoopolis and Oxyrhynchus records. Hydraulis: the Alexandrian coroplastic evidence; Vitruvius 10.8.

nodes.label: Ptolemy's synthesis
nodes.full: Claudius Ptolemy, working at Alexandria, produced the definitive ancient treatments of nearly every mathematical science. The Almagest built a geometric model of the heavens, with epicycles and equants, that predicted the planets well enough to stand for fourteen centuries. The Geography gave coordinates for some 8,000 places and rules for map projection. The Tetrabiblos systematised astrology; further works covered optics, harmonics and the theory of the calendar. It was the high-water mark of Greek exact science.
nodes.src: Almagest: G.J. Toomer's translation (1984). Geography: J. Lennart Berggren & Alexander Jones (2000). Overview: Alexander Jones (ed.), Ptolemy in Perspective (2010).

nodes.label: Alexandria, the school of the doctors
nodes.full: Long after human dissection ended, Alexandria remained the place to train as a physician: it kept teaching skeletons and an anatomical curriculum, and students came from across the empire. The young Galen studied there around 152–157 and drew on its texts for his own huge output, which carried the Alexandrian medical synthesis into Byzantium and, through Arabic, into medieval Europe. 'Alexandrian' stayed a byword for medical authority for five hundred years.
nodes.src: Galen, On Anatomical Procedures 1; On My Own Books. Vivian Nutton, Ancient Medicine (2004) pp.202–06; Heinrich von Staden, Herophilus (1989) on the earlier tradition and its afterlife.

nodes.label: The birth of alchemy
nodes.full: Alchemy was born in Greco-Roman Egypt from the marriage of Egyptian workshop craft — metal alloying, gilding, dyeing, glassmaking — with Greek theories of matter and a language of mystical transformation. Bolus of Mendes wrote recipe-and-theory under the name of Democritus; Maria the Jewess of Alexandria devised distillation apparatus and the gentle heated water-bath still called the bain-marie; and the tradition, continued by Zosimos of Panopolis, framed the transmutation of base metal into gold as an image of the soul's purification.
nodes.src: Marcelin Berthelot, Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs (1888). Recent work: Matteo Martelli, The Four Books of Pseudo-Democritus (2013); Kyle Fraser and others. Maria: quoted in Zosimos.

nodes.label: The Museum after its golden age
nodes.full: The Museum survived into Roman times as an institution of honour: membership, with its stipend and free meals, was granted by the emperor to favoured scholars and public figures across the provinces, not always resident in Alexandria. The scholarship it produced turned increasingly to compilation, commentary and the epitome. The destruction of the Brucheion quarter in Aurelian's reconquest of 272 wrecked the original buildings, and learning shifted to the library at the Serapeum and to private teachers.
nodes.src: Membership as imperial honour: the inscriptions (e.g. IGRR I 1074). The Brucheion: Ammianus 22.16.15; Epiphanius, De mensuris 11. Roy MacLeod (ed.), The Library of Alexandria (2000) pp.61–77.

nodes.label: The Alexandrian roots of Neoplatonism
nodes.full: The philosophy that dominated the late antique mind was assembled at Alexandria. Ammonius Saccas, a shadowy self-taught teacher, drew a circle that included both a Christian and a pagan Origen and the young Plotinus, born at Lycopolis around 204. Plotinus studied with Ammonius for eleven years before leaving for Rome to develop, in the Enneads, the system of the One, Intellect and Soul — Neoplatonism — that would shape Christian, Jewish and Islamic thought for a millennium.
nodes.src: Porphyry, Life of Plotinus. Plotinus, Enneads. Pierre Hadot, Plotinus, or the Simplicity of Vision (1993); Mark Edwards, 'Ammonius, Teacher of Origen', JEH 44 (1993).

nodes.label: Hero of Alexandria
nodes.full: Hero of Alexandria wrote the fullest ancient handbooks of applied mechanics. The Pneumatica describes devices worked by air, steam and water pressure — including the aeolipile, a sphere spun by escaping steam, and a coin-operated dispenser of temple water. The Dioptra sets out a precise sighting instrument and shows how to drive a tunnel toward a meeting point from both ends. The Metrica and Mechanica cover mensuration, gearing, the lever and the screw. It is the ancient engineering tradition at its most complete.
nodes.src: Hero: the Teubner edition (Schmidt, Nix, Schöne, Heiberg, 1899–1914). A.G. Drachmann, The Mechanical Technology of Greek and Roman Antiquity (1963); Serafina Cuomo, Technology and Culture in Greek and Roman Antiquity (2007).

nodes.label: The grain of Rome
nodes.full: Egypt supplied a large share — ancient sources say a third — of the grain that fed the city of Rome, collected as tax in kind, concentrated in the granaries of Alexandria, and carried west each spring and summer by a fleet of large freighters. The sailing was so vital that its timing was public knowledge and a late fleet could mean bread riots in the capital. This was the real reason Egypt was the emperor's closed possession: whoever held Alexandria could starve Rome.
nodes.src: Josephus, Jewish War 2.383, 386. Geoffrey Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980); Peter Garnsey, Famine and Food Supply in the Graeco-Roman World (1988); the Karanis granary ostraca.

nodes.label: The surveyed land and the imperial estates
nodes.full: Every field in Egypt was classified — public, private, temple, or imperial estate — surveyed, and taxed according to the height the flood had reached that year, with the levy paid mostly in wheat into local granaries under officers called sitologoi. Augustus's confiscations of Ptolemaic royal and rebel land created a large bloc of imperial estates (ousiai) run by procurators; over the following centuries this and other land tended to consolidate into big private holdings, the seed of the late-antique great estate.
nodes.src: Dennis Kehoe, Management and Investment on Estates in Roman Egypt (1992); G.M. Parássoglou, Imperial Estates in Roman Egypt (1978). Land survey: P. Tebtunis and the studies of Roger Bagnall.

nodes.label: The Faiyum villages
nodes.full: The drained-lake villages of the Faiyum — Karanis, Tebtunis, Soknopaiou Nesos, Philadelphia — reached their height in the first two centuries: mixed Greek and Egyptian populations, retired soldiers on land grants, orchard and grain farming on irrigated ground, local temples, and constant paperwork with the tax office. Their preserved houses, granaries, tools and vast document dumps are the best evidence anywhere of ancient village life. In the third-century crisis several of them were abandoned for good.
nodes.src: Karanis: the University of Michigan excavations, 1924–35; A.E.R. Boak & E.E. Peterson, Karanis (1931). Tebtunis: the Grenfell–Hunt and Italian excavations. Roger Bagnall & Dominic Rathbone, Egypt from Alexander to the Copts (2004).

nodes.label: The closed coinage and the third-century collapse
nodes.full: Rome kept Egypt a closed currency zone: the Alexandrian mint struck billon tetradrachms that circulated only inside the province, and imperial gold and silver were exchanged at the border. Through the third century the tetradrachm's silver content fell almost to nothing and prices multiplied — one papyrus has a banker instructing his branch to accept 'the divine coinage of the Augusti' despite the rush to spend it. Diocletian's reform of 298 abolished the separate Egyptian coinage after three hundred years.
nodes.src: Angelo Geissen & Wolfram Weiser, Katalog alexandrinischer Kaisermünzen (1974–83). The 'divine coinage' letter: P. Oxy. XII 1411 (260 AD). Kevin Butcher & Matthew Ponting on the debasement metallurgy.

nodes.label: The town economy and the guilds
nodes.full: The nome capitals were manufacturing towns — weaving and dyeing above all, plus oil-pressing, pottery, metalwork, brewing and building. Workers in each trade were organised into guilds with, in many cases, compulsory membership and collective liability for the trade's taxes and for supplying goods and labour to the state. Alexandria's glass, fine linen and papyrus were exported across the empire; Egypt was as much a workshop as a farm.
nodes.src: Guilds: Imre Fikhman, and the Oxyrhynchus and Tebtunis guild documents; Philip Venticinque, Honor Among Thieves: Craftsmen, Merchants, and Associations in Roman and Late Roman Egypt (2016).

nodes.label: The imperial quarries of the Eastern Desert
nodes.full: Deep in the Eastern Desert the emperor ran two great quarries as a direct state enterprise: Mons Claudianus for grey granodiorite columns, and Mons Porphyrites for imperial porphyry, the deep-purple stone reserved for emperors. Their workforces of soldiers, paid stoneworkers and some convicts lived in fortified villages supplied by a chain of wells and pack-camel caravans. Monolithic column-shafts of up to 200 tonnes were dragged on timber sleds down purpose-built wadi roads to the Nile and shipped to Rome.
nodes.src: Mons Claudianus: David Peacock & Valerie Maxfield, Survey and Excavation, Mons Claudianus (1997–2006); Hélène Cuvigny (ed.), Mons Claudianus: Ostraca graeca et latina. Porphyrites: Maxfield & Peacock, The Roman Imperial Quarries: Mons Porphyrites (2001).

nodes.label: The monsoon sailing route
nodes.full: Roman-era captains sailing from Egypt's Red Sea ports learned to leave in July, run before the southwest monsoon across the open Indian Ocean, and reach the pepper coast of southern India in about forty days, returning on the reversed winter winds. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea is a working manual of the routes, ports, goods and prices; Strabo reports up to 120 ships a year making the crossing, where under the Ptolemies it had been a handful.
nodes.src: Periplus Maris Erythraei: Lionel Casson's edition and translation (1989). Strabo 2.5.12, 17.1.13. Steven Sidebotham, Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route (2011); Federico De Romanis, The Indo-Roman Pepper Trade (2020).

nodes.label: Extracting and moving imperial stone
nodes.full: Getting a single porphyry column out of the mountains and to Rome was a sustained engineering operation: cut and dressed at the quarry face, levered onto a heavy timber sled, hauled by teams of men and animals down a graded road with passing-bays and slipways, transferred at the Nile to a specially built barge, and again to a seagoing ship at Alexandria. The 'unfinished obelisk' and abandoned column-shafts in the Eastern Desert mark the failures; the columns in Roman churches and palaces are the successes.
nodes.src: Maxfield & Peacock, The Roman Imperial Quarries: Mons Porphyrites (2001); Ben Russell, The Economics of the Roman Stone Trade (2013). The transport wagons: the ostraca of Mons Claudianus.

nodes.label: Perennial irrigation at village scale
nodes.full: By the Roman period the ox-driven pot-wheel (saqiya), the counterpoised shaduf and the water-screw were standard equipment across the Faiyum and the valley, and land contracts routinely specified who was responsible for the machines and the feeder canals. The technology let a field carry two or even three crops a year instead of the single flood harvest — the basis of the agricultural surplus that fed Rome, and a heavy standing maintenance obligation on the farmer.
nodes.src: Thorkild Schiøler, Roman and Islamic Water-Lifting Wheels (1973). Irrigation clauses in leases: Jane Rowlandson, Landowners and Tenants in Roman Egypt (1996); Katja Mueller, Settlements of the Ptolemies (2006) for the Faiyum system's origins.

nodes.label: Alexandrian instruments and machines in use
nodes.full: The devices of the Alexandrian mechanical tradition had practical uses. Surveyors laid out roads, aqueducts and quarry cuts with the dioptra and measured distances with the odometer; force pumps fought fires and drained ships and mine galleries; the water-screw lifted water in the Rio Tinto and other mines; and Alexandria's own aqueduct and honeycomb of rock-cut cisterns kept a city of hundreds of thousands supplied through the dry months.
nodes.src: John Peter Oleson (ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Engineering and Technology in the Classical World (2008). Alexandria's cisterns: the survey work of the Centre d'Études Alexandrines (Jean-Yves Empereur).

nodes.label: Alexandrian glass and luxury craft
nodes.full: Glassblowing, developed on the Levantine coast in the first century BC, was industrialised in the workshops of Roman Egypt, and Alexandria became famous for luxury glass: cast and cut vessels, gold-leaf 'sandwich' bowls, mosaic and cameo glass. The same workshops turned out faience, worked rock crystal and made the tesserae for the Nilotic mosaics fashionable across the empire. Alexandrian glass and Egyptian linen and papyrus were prestige exports from Britain to India.
nodes.src: E. Marianne Stern, Roman Mold-blown Glass (1995) and Roman, Byzantine and Early Medieval Glass (2001). Alexandrian production: the debate summarised in Ian Freestone's compositional studies.

nodes.label: The India trade at its height
nodes.full: Under Rome the Egypt–India trade became a bulk business. Ships out of Berenike and Myos Hormos carried Roman gold and silver coin, wine, glass, coral and worked metal east, and brought back pepper and other spices, gemstones, ivory, tortoiseshell, fine textiles and Chinese silk transshipped through India. Roman coin hoards dot southern India; Pliny complained that the trade drained a hundred million sesterces a year to the east — an exaggeration, but the imbalance was real.
nodes.src: Pliny, Natural History 6.101, 12.84. Roman coins in India: P.J. Turner, Roman Coins from India (1989). Grant Parker, The Making of Roman India (2008); Raoul McLaughlin, The Roman Empire and the Indian Ocean (2014).

nodes.label: The Muziris papyrus
nodes.full: A second-century papyrus, written on both sides, preserves the paperwork of one voyage: a loan agreement for financing a ship called the Hermapollon trading to Muziris in India, and, on the back, a valuation of part of its return cargo — Gangetic nard, ivory, textiles — after the 25 per cent import duty was taken at Alexandria. The single cargo is worth several million sesterces, a fortune, and the document shows the credit, the customs, the camel haulage across the desert and the scale of profit that made the trade worth the risk.
nodes.src: P. Vindob. G 40822 (the 'Muziris papyrus'): Federico De Romanis, The Indo-Roman Pepper Trade and the Muziris Papyrus (2020); earlier, Lionel Casson, 'New Light on Maritime Loans: P. Vindob. G 40822', ZPE 84 (1990).

nodes.label: Life in the desert forts
nodes.full: The chain of small forts (praesidia) that guarded the roads to the Red Sea ports and the quarries have yielded thousands of ostraca — duty rosters, private letters, requisition notes, love-notes to and from the women who lived at the forts. They show mixed, mobile communities of soldiers, quarrymen, merchants, camel-drivers and prostitutes, resupplied by caravan, trading with and occasionally fighting the desert nomads the Greeks called Trogodytes. The desert was not empty but worked.
nodes.src: Hélène Cuvigny (ed.), La route de Myos Hormos (2003) and Rome in Egypt's Eastern Desert (2018); the Krokodilô, Didymoi and Xeron ostraca.

nodes.label: Meroe and the long peace at the cataract
nodes.full: After Petronius's war the frontier at the First Cataract stayed quiet for nearly three centuries. The Twelve-Mile Land south of Aswan was jointly used; Meroïtic pilgrims and priests worshipped at Philae and left inscriptions there; Meroïtic royal envoys visited Roman prefects, and trade in gold, ivory, ebony, slaves and animals for the arena moved north. As Meroe weakened in the third century and the desert Blemmyes and Nobades pushed in, the settled frontier broke down, and Diocletian pulled the border back to Aswan.
nodes.src: László Török, Between Two Worlds: The Frontier Region between Ancient Nubia and Egypt 3700 BC–AD 500 (2009) pp.427–526. Meroïtic inscriptions at Philae: FHN III. Procopius, Wars 1.19 on the withdrawal.

nodes.label: Egypt as antiquity, wonder and the grotesque
nodes.full: Well-off Greeks and Romans sailed up the Nile as tourists — to the pyramids, the Labyrinth, the sacred crocodiles of the Faiyum, and above all the Colossi of Memnon, one of which 'sang' at dawn and is covered in visitors' verse graffiti, including an emperor's court poet. Egypt fed the Roman imagination as the land of unimaginable age and hidden wisdom, and also of the bizarre and disgusting — Juvenal devotes a whole satire to Egyptians eating a neighbour in a village feud. Obelisks were shipped to Rome and Nilotic scenes tiled onto villa floors.
nodes.src: Memnon graffiti: Bernand & Bernand (1960). Juvenal, Satire 15. Tourism: J.-Y. Empereur and the graffiti corpora; Sarah Yeomans and Molly Swetnam-Burland, Egypt in Italy: Visions of Egypt in Roman Imperial Culture (2015).

nodes.label: The end of Egyptian Jewry
nodes.full: Egypt had held the largest Jewish community in the Roman world — the home of the Septuagint and of Philo, deeply engaged with Greek culture. The pogrom of 38, the confiscation of the Temple-tax as a Roman levy after 70, and above all the Diaspora Revolt of 115–117 destroyed it: the papyri show Jewish property seized and redistributed, and Jewish names all but vanish from the Egyptian record for a century afterward. One of antiquity's great cultural communities was effectively erased.
nodes.src: Corpus Papyrorum Judaicarum I–III (Tcherikover, Fuks & Stern, 1957–64). Joseph Mélèze Modrzejewski, The Jews of Egypt from Rameses II to Emperor Hadrian (1995) pp.198–225.

nodes.label: Alexandria, the second city of the empire
nodes.full: With perhaps half a million people, Alexandria was the largest city in the empire after Rome and, in commerce and learning, its rival. It held the tomb of Alexander, the Museum and the great library at the Serapeum, the busiest harbours in the Mediterranean, a mint, and a population — Greek, Egyptian, Jewish, Syrian, and everything the trade routes brought — famous for rioting over an insult, a tax or a bishop. The country of Egypt often seemed a hinterland to its own coastal capital.
nodes.src: Strabo 17.1.6–13; Dio Chrysostom, Oration 32 (the Alexandrian crowd). Christopher Haas, Alexandria in Late Antiquity (1997); P.M. Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria (1972) for the earlier city.

nodes.label: The Nile, the flood and the Nilometer
nodes.full: Everything still turned on the summer flood. Its height was read off graduated Nilometers — the best known cut into the rock at Elephantine — and reported to Alexandria, where it set the year's land-tax assessment; a 'good Nile' was announced on the coinage. When the flood failed, as in 99 AD, famine and unrest followed within the year, and the papyri fill with petitions for tax relief on land the water never reached.
nodes.src: Danielle Bonneau, Le fisc et le Nil (1971) and La crue du Nil (1964). Nilometers: the Elephantine and Roda structures. Nile-flood coin types of Alexandria: the 'good Nile' issues.

nodes.label: The Eastern Desert put to work
nodes.full: Between the Nile and the Red Sea, Rome built a working landscape where there had been only tracks: two great imperial quarries, gold mines, a lattice of guarded roads with dug wells and stone forts every day's march, and the two Red Sea ports at the eastern end. Camel caravans moved stone, grain, water and trade goods across it, and the nomads the Greeks called Trogodytes and Blemmyes were alternately employed, traded with and fought.
nodes.src: Steven Sidebotham, Martin Hense & Hendrikje Nouwens, The Red Land: The Illustrated Archaeology of Egypt's Eastern Desert (2008); Hélène Cuvigny (ed.), Rome in Egypt's Eastern Desert (2018).

nodes.label: Plague and the Roman-Egyptian demography
nodes.full: Two great pandemics reached Egypt with the wider empire: the Antonine Plague from 165–166, and the 'Plague of Cyprian' from about 249. Tax registers record sudden gaps in village populations, remissions on the land of the dead, and rising wages for scarce labour. Against these shocks, the thousands of surviving census returns let historians reconstruct an ordinary Roman-Egyptian demography — life expectancy at birth around twenty-five, near-universal early marriage, and high fertility barely keeping ahead of death.
nodes.src: Roger Bagnall & Bruce Frier, The Demography of Roman Egypt (1994). Plague in the papyri: Kyle Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017); R.P. Duncan-Jones, 'The Impact of the Antonine Plague', JRA 9 (1996).

nodes.label: The village scribe
nodes.full: Petaus son of Petaus served as village scribe for a cluster of Faiyum villages in the 180s, and his working file survives. It includes a sheet on which he practised writing the opening words of his own certifying formula over and over — 'Petaus, village scribe, I have submitted' — getting the spelling wrong. He could sign and file, but not really read. He is a sharp reminder that the machinery of the best-documented ancient state was run, at the bottom, by the barely literate.
nodes.src: The archive of Petaus: Ursula Hagedorn et al., Das Archiv des Petaus (P. Petaus) (1969). Herbert Youtie, 'ΒΡΑΔΕΩΣ ΓΡΑΦΩΝ: Between Literacy and Illiteracy', GRBS 12 (1971).

nodes.label: The soldier and his family
nodes.full: An auxiliary or legionary posted to Egypt could not legally marry while serving, but in practice kept a household near his base, fathered children, and on discharge received Roman citizenship, a cash bounty or land, and legitimation of his family. Veterans clustered in villages like Karanis, and their archives — enlistment papers, pay records, wills, and letters home like the young recruit Apion's cheerful note from the fleet at Misenum — trace the army as a route out of Egyptian village life and into the Roman order.
nodes.src: Apion's letter: BGU II 423. Soldiers' archives: the dossier of the veteran Lucius Bellienus Gemellus (P. Fay.); Sara Phang, The Marriage of Roman Soldiers (2001); Richard Alston, Soldier and Society in Roman Egypt (1995).

nodes.label: Philo of Alexandria
nodes.full: Philo was the leading intellectual of Alexandrian Jewry: a philosopher who read the Torah, in its Greek version, as an allegory of the soul's journey, harmonising Moses with Plato and the Stoics in a way that would shape Christian theology far more than later Jewish thought. He came from the city's Jewish aristocracy — his brother was the tax-farmer Alexander, his nephew Tiberius Julius Alexander became prefect of Egypt — and in old age he led the community's embassy to the emperor Gaius after the pogrom of 38.
nodes.src: Philo's works, esp. On the Creation, Allegorical Interpretation, In Flaccum, Legatio. Maren Niehoff, Philo of Alexandria: An Intellectual Biography (2018).

nodes.label: Plotinus of Lycopolis
nodes.full: Plotinus was born at Lycopolis in Upper Egypt around 204. He found his teacher in the Alexandrian Ammonius Saccas and stayed eleven years, joined the emperor Gordian's Persian expedition hoping to learn Eastern philosophy (it failed; he barely escaped), and settled in Rome to teach. His pupil Porphyry says he seemed 'ashamed to be in a body' and would never sit for a portrait. The system he built there, of the One overflowing into Intellect and Soul, is the foundation of Neoplatonism.
nodes.src: Porphyry, Life of Plotinus. Plotinus, Enneads (Armstrong's Loeb). Lloyd Gerson (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Plotinus (1996).

nodes.label: The women of the papyri
nodes.full: Egyptian women of the Roman period appear constantly in the documents as economic and legal actors: owning and farming land, lending money at interest, running weaving businesses, going to court, dividing inheritances, and heading households. Roman law required a woman to act through a male guardian for formal transactions, but the papyri show the requirement often reduced to a signature, and a woman with three children could be exempted from it entirely under Augustus's law. Their marriages, dowries, divorces and disputes are documented in unusual detail.
nodes.src: Jane Rowlandson (ed.), Women and Society in Greek and Roman Egypt: A Sourcebook (1998); Roger Bagnall & Raffaella Cribiore, Women's Letters from Ancient Egypt (2006).

nodes.label: The martyrs and Bishop Dionysius
nodes.full: The persecutions produced Egypt's first Christian heroes and its first crisis of authority. Under Severus in 202 died Leonides, the father of Origen, and the young Potamiaena with the soldier Basilides who spared her. Half a century later, Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria wrote circulating letters describing the Decian terror of 250 — the queues to sacrifice, the tortured and the lapsed — and then the plague that followed, in which Christians who nursed the dying 'took the sickness on themselves'. Others, like Antony around 270, answered the age by walking into the desert.
nodes.src: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica 6.1–5, 6.40–42, 7.22 (Dionysius's letters). The Passion of Potamiaena. Athanasius, Life of Antony 1–3.
